items.title: Amazon CloudFront now supports AWS Lambda Web Functions as an origin
items.summary:
Starting today, you can deliver web applications built on AWS Lambda Web Functions through CloudFront's global edge network.  
With CloudFront in front of a Lambda Web Function, you get TLS termination at the edge for lower latency and faster connections, caching for better performance, and custom domains with managed TLS certificates. No changes to application code are needed. CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC) restricts your Lambda Web Function so it's reachable only through CloudFront, so unintended requests that bypass your security protections do not reach your origin. With OAC in place, CloudFront's edge network protects your Lambda Web Function from network-layer DDoS attacks, and you can attach AWS WAF for additional application-layer security. For applications that authenticate their own users, OAC ensures that original credentials reach the application unchanged, so existing sign-in flows keep working.
CloudFront support for AWS Lambda Web Functions is available worldwide, except in the CloudFront China region. To get started, use the CloudFront Console, SDK, CLI, or CloudFormation to configure your Lambda Web Function as a CloudFront origin. For more information, refer to the CloudFront Developer Guide. There are no additional fees associated with this feature.

items.title: Announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions
items.summary: AWS Lambda Web Functions is a serverless compute primitive that runs your HTTP framework natively, delivering fast, consistent responses through multi-concurrent execution and automated global distribution.

items.title: Amazon EC2 G7 instances now available in Europe (Frankfurt) and Europe (Stockholm) Regions
items.summary:
Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) G7 instances powered by NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs are now available in Europe (Frankfurt) and Europe (Stockholm) Regions. G7 instances deliver up to 4.6x AI inference performance and up to 2.1 graphics performance compared to G6 instances. G7 instances also deliver faster performance for GPU-accelerated data analytics workloads.
Customers can use G7 instances for deploying AI models for language translation, video and image analysis, speech recognition and recommender systems. They also accelerate graphics workloads such as creating and rendering real-time, cinematic-quality graphics and game streaming. Additionally, G7 instances support video transcoding, spatial computing, and data analytics workloads. G7 instances feature up to 8 NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs with 32 GB of memory per GPU and custom Intel Xeon 6 processors. They support up to 192 virtual CPUs (vCPUs) and up to 700 Gbps of Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking bandwidth. They also support up to 768 GiB of system memory, and up to 7.6 TB of local NVMe SSD storage.
You can use G7 instances for Amazon EC2 in the following AWS Regions: US West (Oregon), US East (N. Virginia, Ohio) and Europe (Spain, Frankfurt, Stockholm). You can purchase G7 instances as On-Demand Instances, Spot Instances, or as part of Savings Plans.
To get started, visit the AWS Management Console, AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), and AWS SDKs. To learn more, visit the G7 instance page.

items.title: Amazon Connect Customer now prefills step-by-step guides for after contact work
items.summary:
Amazon Connect Customer can now fill in the step-by-step guides that agents complete after a contact, using information extracted from customer conversations, such as booking identifiers, claim numbers, and conversation summaries. Managers can set which information populates each form field. Agents can review and submit rather than manually typing in each field, saving time and improving data accuracy during after contact work.
Contact center agents spend time after each contact entering frequently used information into a step-by-step guide. For example, an insurance agent who finishes a claims call might record the customer’s policy number, a summary of the call, and a disposition code. Now, managers can define rules for which information to extract from the conversation and which fields to automatically fill in the guide. The agent can then check the information, make any necessary corrections, and submit the guide, shortening after contact work and reducing data entry errors.
You can use step-by-step guides with information extraction in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London). Contact summaries are also available in Africa (Cape Town).
To learn more and get started, see step-by-step guides in the Amazon Connect Customer administrator guide.

items.title: AWS Lambda announces Lambda Web Functions
items.summary:
AWS Lambda announces Lambda Web Functions, a new serverless compute primitive where your code handles HTTP requests directly. Your code listens on a port and handles requests as it would on any HTTP server. You use frameworks you already know, such as Express or Hono, with no adapters or custom configuration. This enables you to serve workloads such as AI inference endpoints, server-side rendered (SSR) web apps, streaming API endpoints, microservices, and webhooks. You pay for active CPU time and the memory your environment holds, not for idle CPU time your code spends waiting on databases or downstream services. With this launch, we are also renaming existing Lambda functions to Lambda Event Functions, a naming change only that requires no code changes or redeployments for your existing functions.
Builders use Lambda to go from code to production quickly and without managing servers, across event-driven pipelines, request-response APIs, and data processing. As AI-driven development accelerates, they want to build locally and deploy with a familiar programming model and pay for workloads based on active CPU usage, while serving users with low latency. Lambda Web Functions delivers this. Today, Lambda Web Functions supports the Node.js runtime. A single warm execution environment can serve multiple concurrent requests, which reduces cold starts by orders of magnitude. You can stream results to clients incrementally with native HTTP streaming.
You can create and configure Lambda Web Functions using the AWS Lambda API, Agent Toolkit for AWS, AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS CloudFormation, AWS SAM, AWS CDK, or the AWS SDKs. With multi-Region routing, you can deploy once and serve each request from the Region closest to the end user. Web Functions support Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) connectivity, allowing your function to access resources that exist within a VPC.
Lambda Web Functions is available today in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). For the current list, see the AWS Capabilities by Region page. To learn more, see the Lambda Web Functions developer guide. For pricing details, see AWS Lambda Pricing.  To see Lambda Web Functions in action, see the AWS News Blog announcement.

items.title: Announcing consumption-based pricing for short-term memory in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.summary:
Announcing consumption-based pricing for short-term memory in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory now prices short-term memory (STM) based on the data your agents ingest, retrieve, and store, replacing the previous flat rate per event. AgentCore memory gives agents in-session context through short-term memory and persistent knowledge across sessions through long-term memory. With consumption-based pricing, developers building agents that write frequent, small events pay in proportion to what they use.
STM is priced across three dimensions: ingestion at $1.00 per GB, retrieval at $0.20 per GB, and storage at $0.10 per GB-month. Ingestion and retrieval are billed per event with a 12 KB minimum and 64 KB maximum billable size, while storage is billed on each event's actual size. Most workloads see lower costs, with small-payload use cases seeing the largest reductions. You can manage storage costs by setting a shorter time to live (TTL) on your memory resources. Long-term memory pricing is unchanged.
Consumption-based pricing for AgentCore Memory short-term memory is available in all AWS Regions where AgentCore Memory is offered. To get started, visit the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing page.

items.title: Agentic antimicrobial resistance surveillance with AWS HealthOmics and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.summary: This post presents a reference architecture that turns public sequencing data into plain-language answers about antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes. It pairs AWS HealthOmics for managed genomics processing with a grounded Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent, so researchers can ask questions without writing bioinformatics code or SQL.

items.title: AWS Transfer Family supports custom ports for public SFTP servers
items.summary:
AWS Transfer Family now lets you configure custom ports on public SFTP servers and choose a communication mode for each port. You can support clients that require different ports or start SFTP connections differently on a single server.
Previously, public SFTP servers accepted connections only on port 22 and used server-first communication. With this launch, you can configure up to three ports (22, or any port from 2000 to 65535), allowing you to use the port numbers your business or network requires and offer multiple ports on one server. Some SFTP clients initiate communication themselves, and their connections can occasionally stall on a server-first port. For each port, you can now select client-first or server-first communication and direct clients to the port that matches their connection behavior. Using a port other than 22 can also reduce unwanted connection attempts from automated scanners that target port 22.
This capability is available in all AWS Regions where Transfer Family public SFTP servers are offered. To get started, visit the AWS Transfer Family console or use the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs. To learn more, visit Create an SFTP-enabled server in the AWS Transfer Family User Guide

items.title: Amazon S3 Express One Zone is now available in 4 additional AWS Regions
items.summary:
The Amazon S3 Express One Zone storage class is now available in 4 additional AWS Regions: Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Jakarta), Asia Pacific (Hong Kong), and Africa (Cape Town).
Amazon S3 Express One Zone is a high-performance, single-Availability Zone storage class purpose-built to deliver consistent single-digit millisecond data access for your most frequently accessed data and latency-sensitive applications. S3 Express One Zone delivers data access speed up to 10x faster and request costs up to 80% lower than S3 Standard. It enables workloads such as machine learning training, interactive analytics, and key-value caching in AI search engines to achieve fast data access with high durability and availability.
With this expansion, S3 Express One Zone is now available in 19 AWS Regions. For pricing details, visit the S3 pricing page. To learn more, visit the product page and documentation.

items.title: AWS Secrets Manager adds managed external secrets support for Databricks and Twilio
items.summary:
AWS Secrets Manager now extends its managed external secrets capability to include Databricks and Twilio, enabling you to automatically rotate the credentials that your data pipelines and messaging applications use to call these services. You set up rotation directly from the AWS Management Console or API without writing or maintaining any custom rotation Lambda functions.
Long-lived credentials often stay unrotated because rotation is hard to set up and hard to distribute safely to the applications that use the updated credential. With managed external secrets, you can use Secrets Manager to rotate the Databricks personal access tokens that your jobs and continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines use. You can also rotate the service principal OAuth client secrets that your automation workflows use. Each replacement personal access token retains the scopes of the token it replaces, so a narrowly scoped token stays narrowly scoped.
For Twilio, you can use Secrets Manager to rotate the API keys and Auth Tokens that your applications use to send messages and place calls. For both services, you store the credential in Secrets Manager as a managed external secret and set a rotation schedule. Secrets Manager always returns the current credential, so your applications pick up rotated values automatically, with no code changes required.
These integrations join existing managed external secrets support for BigID, Cisco Security Platform, Confluent Cloud, Datadog, GitLab, Jenkins, MongoDB Atlas, Netskope, Paddle, Salesforce, Snowflake, and SonarQube.
Databricks and Twilio managed external secrets are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Secrets Manager managed external secrets is supported. To learn more, visit the  AWS Secrets Manager managed external secrets documentation.

items.title: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey introduces ElastiCache Insights
items.summary:
Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey now features ElastiCache Insights, a pre-built dashboard in Amazon CloudWatch for your node-based clusters. ElastiCache Insights brings cluster health, memory, compute, network, command throughput, latency, keyspace, and errors into a single view sourced from a set of OpenTelemetry metrics that ElastiCache publishes automatically.
You can use ElastiCache Insights to check the health of your cache workloads across a Region at a glance, detect when a node nears its memory, network, or connection limits, and filter your view to a cluster, shard, node, or Availability Zone. You can also save a copy as the starting point for a custom dashboard tailored to your workload.
With detailed monitoring, you can choose metrics to publish every 15 seconds and view them on the Metrics tab or in your custom dashboard. CloudWatch pricing for OpenTelemetry metrics applies to ElastiCache detailed monitoring.
To get started, open the Metrics tab for a cluster in the Amazon ElastiCache console and choose View in ElastiCache Insights. You can also choose ElastiCache Insights under Infrastructure Monitoring in the Amazon CloudWatch console.
ElastiCache Insights is available for node-based Valkey clusters in all AWS Regions where Amazon CloudWatch supports OpenTelemetry metrics. To learn more about ElastiCache Insights, see Monitoring ElastiCache with OpenTelemetry metrics in the Amazon ElastiCache User Guide.

items.title: Amazon EMR now supports native data quality checks in Apache Spark jobs
items.summary:
Amazon EMR now validates data quality natively within Apache Spark jobs. Data engineering teams can catch quality issues inline before bad data reaches downstream systems, without building or maintaining separate validation infrastructure. Amazon EMR Data Quality, powered by AWS Glue, is available at no additional cost and uses the same declarative rules language (Data Quality Definition Language) and APIs as AWS Glue for a consistent experience across both engines, and works with Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi, and Delta Lake across EC2, EKS, and Serverless deployment modes.
With this feature, you can author validation rules in your Spark scripts or reference rules stored in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, and then apply them at any stage of your pipeline i.e., after reading data, during transformation, or after processing. With 30+ rule types, including dynamic rules that compare against historical runs and ML-based anomaly detection for tracking drift over time without specifying fixed thresholds, Amazon EMR Data Quality provides the flexibility of choosing the validation framework that fits your needs. You can take actions like failing a pipeline, filtering invalid records, or routing them to quarantine based on the quality evaluation results. Results are produced at the dataset, rule, and row level, so that you can easily identify which records or rules are driving the quality failures.
Amazon EMR Data Quality is available on AWS runtime for Apache Spark (emr-spark-8.1.0) in all AWS Commercial, AWS GovCloud (US), and AWS China Regions.
To get started, visit Amazon EMR Data Quality documentation and add DQDL rules for data quality validation to the Spark scripts of your EMR workloads.

items.title: Amazon OpenSearch Service now supports index-level encryption
items.summary:
Amazon OpenSearch Service now supports index-level encryption, letting you encrypt each index at rest with its own AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. This helps you protect data with different ownership or sensitivity under separate keys on the same domain. For example, you can encrypt each tenant's data with its own key in a multi-tenant application.
Index-level encryption builds on the existing encryption at rest capability in Amazon OpenSearch Service. To enable it, set the encryption mode to Native and specify a customer managed AWS KMS key when you create a new domain using the AWS Management Console or the AWS CLI. You can then register additional keys with the domain and use them to encrypt individual indexes.
Index-level encryption is available for domains running OpenSearch version 3.3 or later in 14 AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Seoul, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London, Paris), and South America (São Paulo). There is no additional charge for the feature. Standard AWS KMS and OpenSearch Service charges apply.
To get started, see Index-level encryption in the Amazon OpenSearch Service Developer Guide.

items.title: AWS now lets customers sign up for AWS and pay invoices using ACH direct debit
items.summary:
Starting today, AWS customers in the United States can use a US bank account to sign up for AWS and pay for their AWS services through ACH direct debit. This feature provides a convenient and secure way to manage AWS payments directly from a USD bank account.
Customers can securely connect a personal or business US bank account and use it to pay AWS invoices. Previously, new AWS customers needed a credit or debit card to complete signing up for an account.
During sign-up, customers can choose Bank Account on the AWS sign-up page, select their bank, and authenticate using their bank's mobile app or online banking credentials. This securely verifies ownership and links their bank account to their AWS account. By default, the account will be used to pay future AWS invoices.
Existing customers can add a bank account from the Payment preferences page in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. They choose Add payment method, select Link your bank account, and follow the same bank-selection and authentication flow. Once verified, the bank account is available as a payment method to pay future AWS invoices..
ACH direct debit is available at no additional cost to AWS customers for USD bank accounts. To learn more, see Managing ACH direct debit.

items.title: AWS Security Hub now exports findings to S3 in CSV or JSON format
items.summary:
Today, AWS Security Hub announces support for exporting findings to Amazon S3 in CSV or JSON (OCSF) format. Security teams that need findings outside the console for use cases such as compliance reporting and audit evidence can now export findings from every findings page in the Security Hub console, including Threats, Exposure, Vulnerabilities, Posture Management, Sensitive Data, and All Findings, without building and maintaining their own extraction pipelines.
With this launch, you can start an export on demand from the findings page you are viewing and have Security Hub deliver the results to an S3 bucket in your account. You can choose CSV when you want to review or share findings in a spreadsheet or export in JSON if you need these findings in Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) format.
Findings export is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Security Hub is available. To learn more, visit the AWS Security Hub User Guide at https://docs.aws.amazon.com/securityhub/latest/userguide/securityhub-v2-findings-export.html.

items.title: Amazon EC2 R8gd instances are now available in additional regions
items.summary:
Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) R8gd instances are available in AWS European Sovereign Cloud (Germany) region. These instances feature up to 11.4 TB of local NVMe-based SSD block-level storage and are powered by AWS Graviton4 processors, delivering up to 30% better performance over Graviton3-based instances. These instances are built on the AWS Nitro System and are a great fit for applications that need access to high-speed, low latency local storage. 
 
To learn more, see R8gd instances. To explore how to migrate your workloads to Graviton-based instances, see AWS Graviton Fast Start program. To get started, see the AWS Management Console.

items.title: Amazon EC2 R8g instances now available in additional regions
items.summary:
Starting today, Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) R8g instances are available in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud (Germany) region. These instances are powered by AWS Graviton4 processors and deliver up to 30% better performance compared to AWS Graviton3-based instances. Amazon EC2 R8g instances are ideal for memory-intensive workloads such as databases, in-memory caches, and real-time big data analytics. These instances are built on the AWS Nitro System, which offloads CPU virtualization, storage, and networking functions to dedicated hardware and software to enhance the performance and security of your workloads.
AWS Graviton4-based Amazon EC2 instances deliver the best performance and energy efficiency for a broad range of workloads running on Amazon EC2. AWS Graviton4-based R8g instances offer larger instance sizes with up to 3x more vCPU (up to 48xlarge) and memory (up to 1.5TB) than Graviton3-based R7g instances. These instances are up to 30% faster for web applications, 40% faster for databases, and 45% faster for large Java applications compared to AWS Graviton3-based R7g instances. R8g instances are available in 12 different instance sizes, including two bare metal sizes. They offer up to 50 Gbps enhanced networking bandwidth and up to 40 Gbps of bandwidth to the Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS). 
 
Amazon EC2 R8g Instances. To explore how to migrate your workloads to Graviton-based instances, see AWS Graviton Fast Start program and Porting Advisor for Graviton. To get started, see the AWS Management Console.

items.title: Amazon Bedrock now supports reasoning summaries for OpenAI models
items.summary:
Amazon Bedrock now supports the reasoning.summary parameter for OpenAI models through the Responses API. This capability lets you request a human-readable summary of a model’s reasoning alongside its response, helping you understand its approach to complex tasks such as coding, analysis, and multi-step problem solving.
Reasoning summaries give developers additional context for evaluating responses, debugging applications, and showing users how a model approached a request. The summary is returned in the summary array of the reasoning output item, alongside the model’s answer.
This capability is available for all OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock in all AWS Regions where OpenAI GPT models are available, including in-Region inference, geographic (GEO) cross-Region inference, and global cross-Region inference.
To learn more, see the OpenAI documentation on reasoning summaries. To get started with OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock, see documentation here.

items.title: Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5 are now available on Kiro in AWS GovCloud (US)
items.summary:
Two new Anthropic models are now available in the Kiro IDE and CLI for the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.
Claude Opus 5.5 is Anthropic's most capable Opus model yet and a step up from Opus 5 on long-running agentic coding work. Opus 5.5 thinks adaptively on every request, deciding how much effort each task needs, and completes tasks with roughly 40% fewer tool calls and about half the tokens of Opus 5 in Kiro's internal benchmarking. Available with a 1M context window and 2.0x credit multiplier, down from Opus 5's 2.2x.
Claude Sonnet 5.5 is Anthropic's fastest Sonnet model to date and a natural upgrade for teams already building on Sonnet 5. Output is more than 30% faster, real-world coding and knowledge work approaches Opus 5.5 performance, and clearer writing makes it a stronger collaborator, giving developers a cost-performance dial between maximum capability and higher throughput. Available with a 1M context window and 1.3x credit multiplier.
Ensure your IDE or CLI is updated to the latest version, then restart it to access the new models from the model selector. For more details, visit the GovCloud documentation, the monitoring and tracking guide, or contact your AWS account team. To learn more about Kiro, visit the Kiro product page.

items.title: Amazon Connect Customer now provides automated checks to improve performance evaluation forms
items.summary:
Amazon Connect Customer now suggests changes to performance evaluation forms that improve the accuracy of evaluations automatically filled by AI. While setting up an evaluation form, managers can run an automated check that compares the form against best practices with a single click. Managers then receive a list of evaluation questions that are missing context for AI to score reliably, along with suggestions to make them more specific. For example, the check might flag "Did the agent provide a sales disclosure?" and prompt the manager to define exactly what the agent must disclose before a sale. This helps managers automatically score human and AI agents fairly and accurately, while spending less time refining their evaluation forms.
This feature is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). To learn more, please visit our documentation and our webpage. For information about Amazon Connect Customer pricing, please visit our pricing page.

items.title: Amazon S3 Vectors metadata pre-filtering is now available in AWS GovCloud (US) Regions
items.summary:
Amazon S3 Vectors metadata pre-filtering is now available in the AWS GovCloud (US-East) and AWS GovCloud (US-West) Regions. Pre-filtering evaluates metadata filters before running similarity search, returning up to 5x more of the matching vectors when your filter is selective. S3 Vectors also adds a prefix match operator ($startsWith) for filtering on values like paths and URLs. Together, these improvements give your retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), agentic, and semantic-search applications more complete results when you filter, so your applications return more relevant answers.
S3 Vectors provides native support to store and query vectors in Amazon S3, delivering purpose-built, cost-optimized vector storage and query at billion-vector scale. With this launch, indexes in new vector buckets in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions use metadata pre-filtering by default, with no change to how you write vectors with PutVectors or run filtered queries with QueryVectors. To use pre-filtering on an existing index, update it in place with the UpdateIndexMode API. You can also compare pre-filtering against your current filtering on the same index, using a per-query parameter on QueryVectors, before you update.
Metadata pre-filtering is available at no additional cost in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon S3 Vectors is available, and in the AWS China Regions. We are in the process of deploying this change and plan to complete the deployment in the coming days. To get started, use the AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or the Amazon S3 console. To learn more, visit the Amazon S3 Vectors documentation and the AWS News blog.

items.title: AWS Lambda supports OAuth authentication for self-managed Apache Kafka event sources
items.summary:
AWS Lambda now supports OAuth authentication for self-managed Apache Kafka event source mappings (ESM), including Kafka clusters that customers run themselves and managed offerings such as Confluent Cloud, Aiven, and Redpanda. With this launch, customers can authenticate their Lambda Kafka consumers through their enterprise identity provider, helping them meet the security and compliance requirements for their Kafka applications.
Customers building event-driven Kafka workloads for use cases such as payment processing, fraud detection, and real-time data pipelines use Kafka ESM to build serverless Kafka consumers. Kafka ESM provides automatic scaling, error handling, batching, and event filtering. Previously, Kafka ESM supported only SASL/PLAIN, SASL/SCRAM, and mutual TLS (mTLS) as authentication methods, so customers in regulated industries that require OAuth could not use Kafka ESM with their clusters. With OAuth support, customers can use their enterprise identity provider, such as Amazon Cognito or Okta, to authenticate their Kafka ESM and apply the same identity governance and access policies across their Kafka clusters and Lambda consumers.
This capability is available in all AWS commercial Regions where self-managed Kafka ESM is available. To use OAuth authentication, create a new Kafka ESM with your authentication configuration through the AWS Management Console, Lambda API, AWS CLI, AWS CloudFormation, or AWS SAM. To learn more, see the AWS Lambda developer guide and AWS Lambda pricing.

items.title: Amazon Quick now supports brand templates for on-brand presentations and documents
items.summary:
Starting today, you can upload brand templates in Amazon Quick, allowing you to create presentations and documents that match your approved visual identity. Brand managers set up a template once and everyone gets on-brand output, without hunting for the right file in each chat.
Brand managers upload PowerPoint or Word templates, or pull them from a connected file store such as SharePoint. Quick extracts the colors, fonts, logos, layouts and brand rules from each file. A brand manager reviews and edits what Quick found before publishing it to the whole organization.
Quick also follows a template's rules as it creates new assets. If a request breaks a rule, Quick explains why and suggests an on-brand alternative. For each task, Quick picks the best-fit template based on guidance the brand manager writes. Users can still choose a different template.
Administrators decide who can create and publish brand templates using custom permissions, ensuring that only the proper members of brand, marketing, or other approved teams can set visual standards. 
Brand assets are generally available today in the Amazon Quick desktop app. To learn more, see the Amazon Quick documentation, or create an account for free and start using Quick in minutes.

items.title: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio now supports custom Tooling blueprints
items.summary:
Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio now supports custom Tooling blueprints, giving domain administrators the ability to define the foundation of every project by using their own AWS CloudFormation templates. Administrators can tailor project environments to meet organization-specific requirements, such as IAM role names that comply with company naming standards or custom permissions boundaries instead of AWS managed policies.
Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio administrators start by authoring a CloudFormation template that describes the project environment they need, then register it as a custom Tooling blueprint. The service validates the template at registration and again after each project deployment, confirming that the required resources exist before any team member uses the project. Templates can include any CloudFormation-supported resource, such as AWS Lake Formation grants, Amazon Athena workgroups, or VPC security groups, and work across multiple AWS accounts and Regions without per-project edits. At deployment time, the service automatically populates reserved template parameters, such as the project ID and domain ID, so administrators define the template once and apply it everywhere.
This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio is available. To learn more, visit the Custom blueprints as Tooling documentation.

items.title: TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 model now available on Amazon Bedrock
items.summary:
Amazon Bedrock now supports TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5, a video-to-text model that generates structured, time-coded metadata from video. Until now, finding a moment in a large video library meant knowing where to look before you could ask about it. Pegasus 1.5 reads an entire video and labels what happens and when, turning footage into data your applications can query.
You define what matters to your business, such as editorial segments, speaker changes, sports plays, or brand appearances, and Pegasus 1.5 finds those moments across the video and returns them with timestamps. It analyzes what it sees, hears, and reads on screen in a single pass, with no pre-indexing or ingestion pipeline to build first.
Pegasus 1.5 is accessible through the US and Global cross-Region inference profiles. To get started, visit the Amazon Bedrock product page, access the model in the Amazon Bedrock console, or see the Amazon Bedrock documentation for supported Regions, APIs, features, and pricing.

items.title: OpenAI GPT-6.1 Sol now supports Ultrafast mode on Amazon Bedrock
items.summary:
Today, AWS announces the availability of Ultrafast mode for GPT-6.1 Sol from OpenAI on Amazon Bedrock. Ultrafast mode provides faster inference for workloads where speed matters most. The Amazon Bedrock inference engine delivers the performance, security, and reliability required for production workloads.
Use GPT-6.1 Sol Ultrafast for latency-sensitive applications such as real-time coding assistants, interactive agents, and customer-facing experiences that require fast, high-quality responses. GPT-6.1 Sol helps developers build features, debug issues, investigate complex codebases, and complete multistep workflows. Established AWS controls help you secure workloads, govern access, and audit model invocation activity.
You can get started in the Amazon Bedrock console or programmatically through supported Amazon Bedrock APIs. For information about supported AWS Regions, endpoints, APIs, features, inference profiles, and pricing, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation.

items.title: AWS Cost Explorer, Budgets, and Dashboards now support Amazon Bedrock product attributes
items.summary:
AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, and AWS Cost Management Dashboards now let you analyze Amazon Bedrock costs by product attributes, a new dimension that breaks down Bedrock cost by model, model provider, inference type, and feature. In Cost Explorer and Dashboards, you can group and filter costs by these attributes. In Budgets, you can filter budgets by the same attributes.
With this launch, finance and platform teams get a direct view of which models and workloads drive their Bedrock spend, and can act on it in the billing tools they already use. The attributes include model (such as Claude Sonnet 5 or Claude Haiku 4.5), model provider (such as Anthropic or Cohere), inference type (such as input tokens or output tokens), and feature (such as on-demand inference or reranker). You can combine product attributes with cost allocation tags on application inference profiles, projects, or workspaces to see which applications drive spend on each model, and with IAM principal tags to see which users or roles drive it. Group a month of Bedrock spend by model in Cost Explorer to find your most expensive models, build a dashboard widget that tracks cost per provider, or set a budget that alerts on spend for a single model.
The Amazon Bedrock product attribute dimension is available today at no additional charge in all AWS Regions, excluding the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China (Beijing) and China (Ningxia) Regions. To learn more, see the user guides for Cost Explorer, Budgets, and Dashboards.
